title: Polarized and merged ranges
summary: Which hands bet big, which bet small, and how many bluffs a river bet holds.

what.text:
A **polarized** betting range is very strong hands plus bluffs, with nothing in between. A **merged** (linear) range is strong and medium hands in a row, with almost no bluffs.

Medium hands beat bluffs and lose to strong hands. Betting them big makes little sense: only better hands call, worse ones fold.

size.text:
The bet size follows the shape of the range:
- **Big bets and overbets** go with a polarized range: strong hands want the most money, bluffs want the most folds.
- **Small bets (25–40% pot)** go with a merged range: you get paid by worse hands that call a little, and you protect a medium hand.

Thin value against a calling station is merged too: a small bet it calls with worse.

example.caption: A polarized river bet: the set and the missed draw bet big, the second pair checks.

ratio.text:
How many bluffs a polarized river bet holds so that the opponent can't exploit it by calling or by folding. The bluff share among your bets is **bet / (pot + 2 × bet)**:
- ⅓ pot: 20% bluffs (1 for every 4 value bets).
- ½ pot: 25% (1 to 3).
- ¾ pot: 30%.
- Pot: 33% (1 to 2).
- 2× pot: 40%.

On the flop and turn you can bluff more: those bluffs still have equity to improve.

q-ratio.q: You bet pot on the river with 10 value combos. About how many bluffs keep the bet balanced?
q-ratio.explain: With a pot-sized bet, bluffs are a third of the bets: 1 bluff for every 2 value hands, so 5 for 10.

t1.explain: Big bets suit hands that want either the most money or the most folds.

t2.q: Why is a medium pair rarely bet big on the river?
options: Only better hands call, worse ones fold
t2.explain: A medium hand wins at showdown against bluffs; a big bet turns it into a bluff against better hands.

t3.q: The bluff share of a polarized ½-pot river bet:
t3.explain: 0.5 / (1 + 2 × 0.5) = 25%: one bluff for three value hands.
